full_title: ANONYMOUS, COMPLAINANT, VS. JUDGE ELMER R. BERNARDO, MUNICIPAL TRIAL COURT IN CITIES, BATAC CITY, ILOCOS NORTE, RESPONDENT.
docket: A.M. No. MTJ-26-056 (Formerly JIB FPI No. 23-118-MTJ)
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 1. Standards of Ethical Conduct of Judges and Justices > e. Propriety (Canon IV)
topics: Propriety in a judge's private life (CJCA, Canon IV, Secs. 1-2)
Prejudicial conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service (CJCA, Canon VII, Sec. 18(k))
Retroactive application of the 2025 CJCA to pending cases
Substantial evidence; implausible defense and lack of remorse
Judge's liability as a lawyer (CPRA, Canon II, Sec. 2)
doctrine:
Judges must be beyond reproach in both their public and private lives. Under **Canon IV (Propriety), Sections 1 and 2 of the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (CJCA)**, a judge must freely and willingly accept personal restrictions that an ordinary citizen may find burdensome and must act consistently with the dignity of the judicial office. A judge must also refrain from any act, in or out of court, that may cause dishonor or ridicule to, or tend to tarnish, the judicial office. **A judge may be penalized even for conduct unrelated to official duties when it gravely tarnishes the public image of the Judiciary.**

**A judge who, at around 2:30 a.m., threw a piece of wood and a stone that damaged his neighbors' parked vehicles, then defended himself with an implausible story (that he was aiming at a rat), is guilty of "prejudicial conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service," a serious offense under Canon VII, Section 18(k) of the CJCA.** This offense reformulates "conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service": acts that tarnish the image and integrity of public office without a direct relation to official duties. Even on the judge's own version, recklessly hurling objects where property could be damaged falls below the standard required of judges. An incredible defense, and "background facts" blaming the victims, show lack of remorse and worsen the judge's position.

The CJCA applies to cases pending when it took effect (transitory clause). The quantum of proof is substantial evidence; technical rules do not strictly apply, but the respondent must have a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Under Canon VII, Section 22, a serious offense is punishable by dismissal, suspension, and/or a fine. Where there is a mitigating circumstance such as first offense (Sec. 24) and no aggravating circumstance, the Court may impose a suspension or fine not less than half the minimum (Sec. 25). The Court imposed a fine of PHP 50,001.00. Because a judge is also a lawyer, the Court may separately remind him under Canon II, Section 2 of the CPRA (dignified conduct).
facts:
On August 18, 2023, the Judiciary Public Assistance Section received an anonymous email complaint against Judge Elmer R. Bernardo, Presiding Judge of the MTCC of Batac City, Ilocos Norte. It alleged that while drunk he had hit a tricycle and injured its driver, had damaged about seven vehicles (throwing stones, smashing windshields, and pushing a jeep into a canal), had never paid compensation, and had made a police officer manipulate a blotter entry.

The OCA investigated in October 2023. The anonymous complainant did not answer the OCA's request for a meeting. The OCA obtained a police blotter entry of July 29, 2023: neighbors Allan Paul Paraoan and Richelle Joy Wronski reported that at about 2:30 a.m., Judge Bernardo, allegedly under the influence of liquor, threw a piece of wood and a stone at their parked Ford and Isuzu Crosswind, denting them and detaching their rain visors. They said he admitted the act while being recorded on a cellphone. Paraoan confirmed to the OCA that the blotter was accurate but would not execute an affidavit because he had already settled with the judge. The Batac PNP reported no record of the tricycle incident. The JIB's Office of the General Counsel filed a formal complaint on April 12, 2024 for prejudicial conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service.

Judge Bernardo denied being drunk. He admitted throwing the wood and the stone but said he threw them from his veranda at a rodent "the size of a cat" and hit the vehicles by accident. He said he apologized, paid for the repairs, and that the owners later tried to pad the blotter with unrelated damage. He also added "background facts": his neighbors habitually parked on the narrow street and resented his requests to move their vehicles.

The JIB's Office of the Executive Director found his story hard to believe. In its May 21, 2025 Report, it recommended that he be found guilty, fined PHP 50,001.00, sternly reminded as a member of the Bar under Canon II, Section 2 of the CPRA, and sternly warned. The JIB adopted the report on June 27, 2025. The 2025 CJCA took effect while the case was pending.
issues: Whether the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability governs this case, which was pending when the Code took effect.
Whether Judge Bernardo is guilty of prejudicial conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service for damaging his neighbors' vehicles.
What penalty should be imposed, and whether he should also answer as a member of the Bar.
ruling:
**1. Yes, the CJCA applies.** Its transitory clause makes it applicable to "all pending and future cases," except where retroactive application would not be feasible or would work injustice.

**2. Yes, he is guilty.** Under Canon IV, Sections 1 and 2, a judge must embrace personal restrictions, act consistently with the dignity of the office, and refrain from any act, in or out of court, that may cause dishonor or ridicule to the judicial office. Citing Obiedo v. Santos, the Court stressed that a judge, "[l]ike Caesar's wife," must be above suspicion, and that when a judge becomes a transgressor of the law he places his office in disrepute. **"The law penalizes judges even for conduct which does not relate to the performance of their duties, where their acts gravely tarnish the public image of the Judiciary."**

The quantum of proof is substantial evidence. The anonymous complaint and the police blotter alone did not prove that the judge acted deliberately or was intoxicated. But Paraoan's confirmation, together with the judge's own statements, painted "a vivid picture" of what happened. His story was implausible: he was on his veranda before dawn, a piece of wood and a stone were conveniently there, and he threw twice at a rodent near the very vehicles he had found illegally parked, causing a commotion that woke the neighbors. **Concocting "such a fantastic defense" worsened his position.** His unnecessary "background facts" about his neighbors' parking showed resentment and "utter lack of remorse." It was therefore reasonable to conclude that the incident "was not completely without malice." **Even assuming his version were true, his recklessness in throwing objects where property could be, and was, damaged still fell below the standard required of judges.** It created an appearance of impropriety and diminished public confidence in the Judiciary. The Court warned that when judges escape punishment through legal maneuvering, "it is the judicial institution itself that suffers."

Under Canon VII, Section 18(k), "conduct unbecoming of a judge or prejudicial, vulgar or scandalous conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service" is a serious offense. Its meaning is settled: the Rule 140 annotation (Rule 140 having been superseded by the CJCA) explains that the offense reformulates "conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service," which covers acts that tarnish the image of public office without direct relation to official duties, so that it would not remain a blanket offense.

**3. Fine of PHP 50,001.00; stern reminder as a lawyer.** Under Canon VII, Section 22, serious offenses are punishable by dismissal; suspension of one year and one day to three years; and/or a fine of more than PHP 101,000.00 up to PHP 500,000.00. First offense is a mitigating circumstance (Sec. 24). With a mitigating circumstance and no aggravating circumstance, the Court may impose a suspension or fine not less than half the minimum (Sec. 25). This being his first offense, the Court adopted the JIB's recommended fine of PHP 50,001.00. As to his liability as a lawyer under Canon II, Section 2 of the CPRA (dignified conduct; no scandalous behavior in public or private life), a stern reminder sufficed: only one incident was established, he was already penalized as a judge, and he had expressed remorse and offered reparation.
disposition: Judge Elmer R. Bernardo was found GUILTY of prejudicial conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service and FINED PHP 50,001.00, payable within three months from notice. He was STERNLY REMINDED, as a member of the Bar, to maintain dignified conduct and strictly observe Canon II, Section 2 of the CPRA, and STERNLY WARNED that a repeat of the same or similar offense will be dealt with more severely.

bar_questions.q: Judge Ramos, an MTC judge, came home past midnight and found his neighbor's car parked across his gate, as it often was. In full view of other neighbors, he kicked and dented the car's door and shouted that the owner had no respect for a judge. The next day he paid for the repairs. In the administrative case that followed, Judge Ramos argued that the incident was a purely private quarrel unrelated to his judicial functions, so the Court has no basis to discipline him. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No. Judge Ramos may be disciplined for prejudicial conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service, even though the act was unrelated to his official duties.
alac.legal_basis: Under Canon IV, Sections 1 and 2 of the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability, a judge must accept personal restrictions an ordinary citizen may find burdensome, must act consistently with the dignity of the judicial office, and must refrain from any act, in or out of court, that may cause dishonor or ridicule to, or tend to tarnish, the judicial office. "Prejudicial, vulgar or scandalous conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service" is a serious offense under Canon VII, Section 18(k). It covers acts that tarnish the image of the Judiciary without direct relation to official duties. Judges may be penalized even for conduct unrelated to their duties when it gravely tarnishes the Judiciary's public image. (Anonymous v. Judge Bernardo, A.M. No. MTJ-26-056, February 4, 2026)
alac.application: Kicking and denting a neighbor's car in front of other residents, out of resentment over parking, shows the lack of restraint that Canon IV forbids. That the quarrel was private does not matter: the offense covers acts with no direct relation to official functions, and a judge's private behavior must also be beyond reproach. Paying for the repairs may show remorse, but it does not erase the public spectacle that diminished respect for the judicial office.
alac.conclusion: Judge Ramos is administratively liable despite the private nature of the incident.

bar_questions.q: Judge Velasco threw two stones from his balcony at night. The stones struck and dented two vehicles parked on the street. He claims he was trying to scare off a stray dog and never meant to hit the vehicles. He apologized and paid for the repairs that same week. Assume the investigating body believes his account that the damage was accidental. (a) Is Judge Velasco still administratively liable? (b) If this is his first offense and there is no aggravating circumstance, may the Court impose a penalty below the minimum fine prescribed for the offense?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. Even if the damage was accidental, his reckless conduct falls below the standard required of judges. (b) Yes. With a mitigating circumstance and no aggravating circumstance, the Court may impose a suspension or fine not less than half the minimum prescribed.
alac.legal_basis: In Anonymous v. Judge Bernardo (A.M. No. MTJ-26-056, February 4, 2026), the Court held that even assuming the judge's version (that he threw objects at a rodent and hit the vehicles by accident), "his recklessness in throwing items in an area where private property could be, and was in fact, damaged still constitutes conduct falling below the standard of behavior expected of members of the Judiciary," in violation of Canon IV of the 2025 CJCA. On penalty, Canon VII, Section 24 of the CJCA treats first offense as mitigating. Section 25 allows the Court, where there is one or more mitigating circumstance and no aggravating circumstance, to impose suspension or a fine not less than half the minimum prescribed. Applying these, the Court imposed a fine of PHP 50,001.00 on a first-time offender.
alac.application: Judge Velasco threw stones toward a street where vehicles were parked. No prudent judge would hurl objects that could damage property nearby, so the lack of intent does not excuse him. The incident created an appearance of impropriety and exposed the judicial office to ridicule. His prompt apology and payment, and the fact that this is his first offense, bear on the penalty, not on liability. Since there is a mitigating circumstance (first offense) and no aggravating one, the Court may go below the minimum fine, down to half of it.
alac.conclusion: Judge Velasco is liable, but as a first offender he may be fined an amount not less than half the minimum prescribed.

bar_questions.q: An anonymous email to the Supreme Court accused Judge Cruz of several drunken incidents: hitting a pedestrian, smashing car windshields, and pressuring police to alter blotter entries. The OCA's investigation found a police record of only one incident, in which Judge Cruz damaged a neighbor's car. The neighbor confirmed the blotter entry but refused to execute an affidavit because he had been paid. In his comment, Judge Cruz admitted causing the damage but gave an unbelievable explanation. (a) What quantum of proof is required, and may Judge Cruz be held liable on this record? (b) Being a lawyer, may he also be held to account under the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability?

alac.answer: (a) Substantial evidence is required. Judge Cruz may be held liable for the incident proved by the confirmed blotter entry and his own admissions, but not for the unproven allegations. (b) Yes. As a member of the Bar, he is bound by Canon II, Section 2 of the CPRA, and the Court may also sanction or remind him under it.
alac.legal_basis: In administrative cases against judges, the quantum of proof is substantial evidence: relevant evidence that a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion. Technical rules of procedure and evidence do not strictly apply, but the respondent must have a reasonable opportunity to be heard. In Anonymous v. Judge Bernardo (A.M. No. MTJ-26-056, February 4, 2026), the Court held that an anonymous complaint and a police blotter entry alone did not establish that the judge acted deliberately or was intoxicated. The owner's confirmation of the blotter, together with the judge's own statements, sufficed to hold him liable. Canon II, Section 2 of the CPRA requires a lawyer to act with dignity and not to behave in a scandalous manner, in public or private life, to the discredit of the legal profession. In Bernardo, the Court sternly reminded the judge under this provision, finding that a stern reminder sufficed because only one incident was established, he was already penalized as a judge, and he had shown remorse and offered reparation.
alac.application: The anonymous email, standing alone, does not prove the pedestrian incident or the blotter tampering; those charges fail for lack of substantial evidence. The car-damage incident, however, rests on the blotter entry confirmed by the owner and on Judge Cruz's own admission that he caused the damage. His unbelievable explanation does not help him and may show lack of remorse. That evidence is adequate for a reasonable mind, so he may be held liable for that incident. As a lawyer, his scandalous private conduct also falls under Canon II, Section 2 of the CPRA. The Court may impose a separate sanction or a reminder, depending on the circumstances.
alac.conclusion: Judge Cruz may be held liable on substantial evidence for the proven incident only, and he may also be called to account as a member of the Bar under the CPRA.

notes: Leonen, SAJ., dissented and would have dismissed the judge; the dissent is not examinable. Villanueva, J., took no part; the decision gives no reason, though footnote 7 shows he signed the November 15, 2023 OCA report as Court Administrator. The decision dates the Batac PNP letter to the JIB "February 23, 2023," which comes before the August 18, 2023 complaint; it is probably a typographical error in the source, so the date is left out. On the penalty, the decision quotes the CJCA fine for serious offenses as "more than PHP 101,000.00 but not exceeding PHP 500,000.00" and the half-of-the-minimum rule (Canon VII, Sec. 25). It then adopts the PHP 50,001.00 fine that the JIB had recommended in May 2025, before the CJCA took effect. Remember the amount as imposed and do not try to derive it. The anonymous complaint's other allegations (the tricycle driver, the seven vehicles, the blotter manipulation) were not established.
